title: German Alphabet and Sounds
explanation: German uses the 26 basic Latin letters plus Ä, Ö, Ü, and ß. Learn both the name of each letter for spelling and its common sound inside a word. Some letters can make more than one sound, so always connect the sound to a clear example word.
commonMistakes: Confusing the letter name with the sound the letter makes inside a word.
Pronouncing German W like English W instead of the German /v/ sound.
Pronouncing German Z like English Z instead of /ts/.
Treating Ä, Ö, and Ü as decoration instead of separate vowel sounds.
Writing B instead of ß; ß represents a sharp s sound. The official uppercase ẞ exists, while beginner words normally show lowercase ß.

practice.prompt: Which letter makes the opening /ts/ sound in Zeit?
practice.explanation: German Z normally represents /ts/, so Zeit begins with the same sound as the end of English cats.

practice.prompt: Which letter represents /v/ at the start of Wasser?
practice.explanation: German W is commonly pronounced /v/, unlike English W.

practice.prompt: Which German letter is called Vau?
practice.explanation: V is named Vau; in native German words such as Vater it commonly sounds /f/.

practice.explanation: Q is normally followed by u, and qu is pronounced /kv/ as in Quelle.

practice.explanation: Tür uses Ü, made with rounded lips and the tongue position of German I.

practice.explanation: Ä and ä are the same umlaut vowel in uppercase and lowercase.

title: Richer Concessive Links
explanation: Use auch wenn for a real repeated obstacle, selbst wenn for an extreme or hypothetical obstacle, and zwar...aber to acknowledge one point before contrasting it. Trotz plus a noun compresses the same relationship.

commonMistakes: Using selbst wenn without verb-final order.

title: Unreal Past Conditions
explanation: Use hätte or wäre plus a past participle to imagine a different past. In the result clause, use hätte or wäre as well; with modal verbs, hätte plus a double infinitive is common.
